item.title: The New Kingmakers (2 minute read)
item.description: Revenue scale is no longer sufficient when raising a round. What actually matters is how many top AI-native companies use, love, and embrace your products and profess undying loyalty to you. AI-native companies are the hardest customers to win, so they are the leading indicator. Revenue can be bought, but loyalty from a kingmaker can't be manufactured.

item.title: Pulley, a Carta rival, is shutting down (2 minute read)
item.description: Pulley raised more than $50M to compete with Carta. Now it's shutting down and directing customers to that same competitor. The cap-table startup closes December 8, giving customers about twelve weeks to move. A former employee speculated that spreadsheets, increasingly improved with AI, were a bigger competitive problem than Carta itself. If you use Pulley, start checking the migration details now, especially which records transfer automatically and what you'll need to export yourself.

item.title: The Harness Margin Opportunity (3 minute read)
item.description: The right harness can cut the cost of the same result by 71% without a loss of accuracy. This presents an opportunity for the next generation of software applications. State-of-the-art models can be expensive to use, but a good harness can reduce costs enough for them to be a viable option. An effective harness requires deep customer understanding, a collection of relevant evals, and a factory for automating hill-climbing.

item.title: Inside 12 months of AI search experiments (8 minute read)
item.description: HubSpot spent twelve months testing what gets a company found in AI search. Adding an llms.txt file did nothing, while 92% of its highly specific industry and use-case pages eventually earned citations. A page-speed overhaul increased AI crawler visits by 1,600%, and qualified leads from AI search rose 1,850% over the year. The experiments give teams somewhere concrete to start. Track whether the content brings qualified leads, though, because more crawler visits alone won't tell you whether it's working.

item.title: Why would someone pay for your app when AI does it for free? (16 minute read)
item.description: Your customer can ask ChatGPT for a lesson. Getting them to practice again tomorrow is a different problem. This article suggests comparing your app's main use case with what someone can do in a blank chat window, then looking at what's missing. Does your app remember their progress, organize what comes next, or give them someone to practice with? Those are reasons to keep using it even when the answers are available elsewhere. If you're struggling to explain why someone should pay, try the comparison yourself.

item.title: Column is releasing four new products (3 minute read)

item.title: Reimagining advertising with AI (4 minute read)
item.description: A customer can now ask an ad questions before visiting your website. OpenAI is testing Sponsored Agents with select US advertisers, letting users talk with a business-sponsored agent before clicking through to buy. It's also adding ChatGPT Ads integrations to HubSpot and Shopify. That moves some of the selling into the ad itself. If you get access to the test, your product information and the agent's answers will need as much attention as the creative and landing page.

item.title: Why Does Your Team Think You're a Worse Manager Than You Do? (4 minute read)
item.description: You suggest a new feature during a meeting. A week later, someone has built it, and the project you actually needed is behind. You thought you were sharing an idea, but they thought you were giving them a task. This is one reason founders and their teams can disagree about how well things are managed. Tell people whether you're asking for opinions or assigning work. When you do add a task, explain how it ranks against what they're already doing.

item.title: How to Raise Venture Capital Chapter 1: The Speed Run (13 minute read)
item.description: One investor wants an answer by Friday. Another can't meet until next month. You can end up choosing before you know who else is interested. This fundraising guide explains how to avoid that by building relationships early, then scheduling your pitch meetings close together so investors can reach decisions around the same time. Aim to finish the raise before you're down to six months of cash. Even after you accept a term sheet, investors still need to complete their checks and finalize the paperwork before the money reaches your account.

item.title: Conway's Law Is Dead. Or Is It? (2 minute read)
item.description: Conway's law says that software reflects the communication structures of the organizations that build it. AI is now part of those structures. This means existing workflows need to change, with a focus on outcomes. Human judgment still matters, so alignment therefore involves humans adapting too.

item.title: The Era of Compounding Capital (7 minute read)
item.description: Capital structures now serve as competitive moats, particularly for companies leveraging AI and infrastructure, by transforming financial engineering into a decisive advantage. Startups need strategies to compound capital alongside traction, using each milestone to reduce financial risk and attract diverse funding sources. The most resilient companies use abundant capital to secure more durable sources, ensuring each dollar raised eases future fundraising efforts and propels growth.

item.title: Making Startups Powerful (15 minute read)
item.description: Paul Graham suggests startups should focus on becoming more powerful, not just more profitable. Strategies include owning customer relationships, creating network effects, and transforming into a marketplace or full-stack solution. Helping users make money, being generous, and selling early-stage to fast-deciding customers can also enhance a startup's long-term strength.

item.title: Your playbook for LinkedIn ads that work (16 minute read)
item.description: LinkedIn ads cost $37.42 per thousand impressions against about $10 on Meta, so the playbook starts with when NOT to run them. They only pay off when deal size is at least $10K and there are at least 10,000 decision-makers to reach, with $3,000 a month as the minimum test budget. Instead of targeting by job title, the author pulls buying signals like job postings and tech-stack changes and uploads them as a custom audience. Switching one account to manual bidding took cost per lead from $287 to $90.

item.title: How we built LangChain's Paid Media Agent (19 minute read)
item.description: The strongest results come from giving an agent a well-designed workspace with a sandbox, software, business context, and clear operating instructions. The system prompt becomes a map that helps the agent find what it needs without carrying everything in context. Use models for judgment and code for consistency. Agents need to find the right tools, work within clear permissions, and move from analysis to action. This meant proposing campaign changes, routing them through human approval, and verifying that the changes were applied correctly.

item.title: One Thing Miro + Airtable Show: Getting Cash Flow Positive Isn't Magical (8 minute read)

The cash sat there earning the worst multiple on the cap table.

item.title: From 1 to 100 IRL events in a year: The secret to getting engineers to demo (6 minute read)

More than half the company has now demoed somewhere, and about 95% of those events put them face to face with customers. About 20% of engineers opt out of speaking and nothing happens to them.

item.title: My last six months at Evernote, after Bending Spoons took over (9 minute read)

Bending Spoons later listed at $18.4B. He reads a voluntary severance offer as the new owner announcing its plan for the org.

item.title: AI spend per employee slumped at top firms in August — summer doldrums or a warning sign? (3 minute read)
item.description: Ramp's August card data covers 70,000 companies, and it is the number your board will compare your AI spend against. More than half of companies pay for at least one AI product, but that share barely grew, up 0.4% on July. At the heaviest spenders, spend per employee fell almost 10% to $7,205, and part of that is price. The average cost of a million tokens has dropped to $0.68 from a March peak of $1.15, so the same usage costs less each month. If you sell AI, customers' bills are shrinking without them buying less.

item.description: AI venture markets are pricing early-stage companies as if many could become Anthropic-scale outcomes even as mature software assets sell for modest revenue multiples. That gap is fueling investor anxiety and raising the risk of overpaying for consensus deals.

item.title: The SaaSpocalypse was more like a RenaiSaaS (8 minute read)
item.description: SaaS valuations dropped nearly $2 trillion in early 2026 due to fears about AI disrupting business models, but revenue growth quickly rebounded. The Stripe SaaS Index, measuring weekly pay-in volumes of 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses, showed strong growth post-sell-off, particularly among young companies and in the US market. Healthcare, retail, and professional services sectors outperformed pre-crisis trends, with AI adoption contributing to the resilience, especially among younger firms.

item.title: The Golden Snitch (9 minute read)
item.description: Exceptional performance often comes from finding the one outcome that matters more than assigned tasks. Teams should distinguish visible activity from decisive results, give proven employees autonomy, and identify which achievement would materially change the company's trajectory.

item.title: Ecstatic Highs and Suicidal Lows (3 minute read)
item.description: Startup leaders face volatile emotional swings when teams fall behind critical milestones. Effective leadership requires adapting to the moment: challenge teams during highs, absorb pressure during lows, remove bottlenecks, and choose tools deliberately instead of amplifying stress by default.

item.title: An Ode to Counter-Positioning (15 minute read)
item.description: Counter-positioning allows startups to challenge incumbents by adopting business models that incumbents can't replicate without harming their own profit structures. Examples include Ramp's focus on saving customer money and Base Power's shift from battery sales to electricity services. This strategy buys startups time to develop lasting moats like Scale Economies and Network Effects.

It brings together what agents need to understand the business, reason and plan, take action, and operate within enterprise controls.

PitchBook counts 63 US companies worth $10B or more, up from 26 in 2021, with 19 new ones in the first half of this year. Rounds of $100M or more took 87.5% of the $412.7B invested in that half.
